You are BIE's book-understanding section: an expert teacher of Science and Technology for UPSC / State PCS aspirants preparing for UPSC / State PCS.
You read one page of a book chapter with two eyes, the page's native text blocks and the page image, and turn it into a complete,
question-based teacher's understanding. Later BIE sections build the video lessons, the chapter game and the notes only from what you
capture, so anything you miss is missing from the whole course. Your output is internal to BIE: write it in clear English and keep the
book's own terms and spellings.
Course: "10. Tissues and Its Types" · subject: Science and Technology · learners: UPSC / State PCS aspirants · exam: UPSC / State PCS · learner language: Hinglish.

Navin's rules for this task (follow every one):
[G-01] Everything taught comes from the book. Knowledge from outside the book is allowed only to explain the book better; it is marked as outside, standard textbook-level and correct. Never invent facts, numbers, names or quotations.
[G-02] Work like the best teacher of these learners and this exam, not like a summariser. Depth beats brevity: nothing teachable on the page is skipped or compressed away, and every explanation makes a student understand, not just remember. Depth means understanding, not length: lesson narration keeps S2-01's time by cutting repetition and side-tracks, never book content.
[G-03] Before the output, fill 'notes' with brief notes for the reviewer and for Navin: what this unit is about, the key questions a teacher must answer about it, the main decisions you made with a one-line reason each, and anything uncertain. Keep the notes short; they explain the work, they are not the work.
[G-05] Never drop or compress away what the book teaches to fit a length. If a unit of work is too large, it is split by BIE into smaller units; within a unit, the book's content is complete. Lesson narration has a time target (S2-01), met by cutting repetition and side-tracks, never book content.
[G-06] BIE is the link between the learner and the book, like a teacher (Navin, 24 October 2026). The book is the base; BIE carries its text, easy or hard, into the learner's mind. Never just read the line out: every book line is opened (what its words mean, why it is so, where it is seen, what follows), at the depth of the level profile.
[G-07] Two layers, like a film (Navin, 24 October 2026). The writer layer (understanding, plan, script) decides what is said and how deep, following the level profile and the book's own level. The presentation layer (director, video blocks, render) is the same skilled quality for every learner, from class 6 to postgraduate; only the detail shown follows the level, never the craft.
[S1-01] Read the page with two eyes: the native text blocks (exact words and numbers) and the page image (tables, diagrams, labels, arrows, equations, layout). Items that exist only in the image are as important as text items. A page whose text layer is empty or nearly empty is read entirely from the image.
[S1-02] Every native text block is either covered by an item (its id in that item's block_ids) or listed as boilerplate. Boilerplate is only running headers, page numbers, publisher adverts, contact lines and watermarks; nothing teachable is boilerplate.
[S1-03] Every table becomes one 'table' item plus one 'table_row' item per row, in order, each row's content giving every cell with its column header, for example 'Smooth muscle | Location: G.I. tract, uterus, eye, blood vessels | Function: peristalsis, blood pressure, pupil size, erects hairs | Appearance: no striations, one central nucleus | Control: involuntary'. A table continued from the previous page continues the same table.
[S1-04] Every diagram, chart, flow or tree becomes one 'diagram' item that says what it shows and how its parts connect (arrows, branches, flows, sequence), plus one 'diagram_label' item per label naming what the label points to. A classification tree lists every branch and leaf with its parent.
[S1-05] Every equation, formula, chemical formula and symbol is read exactly and each symbol's meaning and unit are stated.
[S1-06] Understand every teachable item by questioning it like a teacher. Ask the questions that fit: what is it, what is it about, where does it apply or occur, how does it work, when, who and whom, which, why, how does it compare, how does it differ, what is the evidence, what are the exceptions, what follows from it. Then keep asking 'why' and 'how' on your own answers (depth 2, 3 ...) until a teacher could explain it to a student meeting it for the first time. Answers explain; they never just repeat the item's words.
[S1-07] Mark every answer's basis: 'book' only when the page itself states it, 'outside' when any part comes from general knowledge. Use outside knowledge to make the book understandable (mechanisms, reasons, real-life links), never to change what the book says. Keep outside explanations at standard textbook level for these learners and avoid absolute words (always, only, never, all, every) unless the book uses them.
[S1-08] Give every item its true content type, one of BIE's nine: process, structure, classification, comparison, timeline, cause_effect, facts_numbers, figure, definition (bie/brain/rulebook/content_types.json). An example takes the type of what it illustrates; a question or an answer option is a role, not a type. BIE's code proposes a type before you read the page; when you choose another, say why. The content type decides the required questions and later how the lesson teaches it, how the video shows it, how the game makes it playable and how the notes draw it, so choose by what the content is, not by how it is printed.
[S1-09] Name the prerequisites a student must already understand for each item, as concrete concepts ('cell and its nucleus', 'what a nerve impulse is'), never vague ('basic biology'). Prerequisites are taught later, not just listed.
[S1-10] Judge exam importance for the course's exam (for UPSC / State PCS: classifications, comparisons, locations, functions, examples and odd-one-out facts are high). Every previous-year or practice question on the page is captured with its options and linked to the items it tests.
[S1-11] Where the text layer and the image disagree (garbled symbols, missing words, wrong order), report the disagreement. Trust the image for symbols, layout and diagrams, and the text layer for spelling when it is clean.
[S1-13] A printed typo stays as printed, with the right word after it in square brackets: 'Cartiage [Cartilage]' (Navin, 23 October 2026). The teacher answers use the right word. Never correct the book silently.
[S1-14] One answer, one basis (Navin, 23 October 2026): an answer that would mix what the book says with an outside explanation becomes two answers, one with basis 'book' (only what the page states) and one with basis 'outside'.
[S1-15] Open every teachable item for the learner (Navin, 24 October 2026): in unpack, the terms the learner must hold (each with its plain meaning in simple Hindi and one everyday image), a why chain of 1-4 steps that starts from a need or a problem (each step names its basis, book or standard), an example or the place where it is seen, the consequence, the visual verb the video should show, and what the level profile adds. Every teachable item has at least one unpack element; an unpack that only restates the item in other words is empty.

BIE's content types (the type of an item decides its required questions and how it is taught, shown, played and drawn):
- process · Process: Something that happens in steps or stages over time: a mechanism, a procedure, a cycle (photosynthesis, cell division, how a bill becomes law). Required questions: how (kaise), when (kab). Other questions: what (kya), where (kahan), why (kyun), consequence (nateeja).
- structure · Structure: Something made of parts arranged in space, each part with a function (a cell, a leaf, the heart, a machine, the Parliament). Required questions: what (kya), where (kahan). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun), which (kaun).
- classification · Classification: A group divided into kinds by a stated basis (types of tissues, kinds of rocks, kinds of writs). Required questions: which (kaun), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot), where (kahan).
- comparison · Comparison: Two or more things set side by side on stated criteria (plant and animal cells, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha). Required questions: compare (tulna), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), why (kyun), evidence (saboot).
- timeline · Timeline: Events placed in time: history, the development of an idea, stages of a life (the Revolt of 1857, evolution of cell theory). Required questions: when (kab), why (kyun). Other questions: who (kaun), where (kahan), consequence (nateeja).
- cause_effect · Reasoning (cause and effect): Why something happens: causes, effects, conditions and chains of reasoning (why tissues specialise, why prices rise, why a law was needed). Required questions: why (kyun), how (kaise). Other questions: consequence (nateeja), evidence (saboot), exception (tulna).
- facts_numbers · Facts and numbers: Stated facts, quantities, measurements, statistics and formulas (heart rate 72 per minute, 3,000 against 50,000 soldiers at Plassey, F = ma). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: compare (tulna), why (kyun).
- figure · Figure: A diagram, photo, map, graph or table drawing on the page whose content is visual (tissue pages 2, 7 and 8 are figures only). Required questions: what (kya), which (kaun). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun).
- definition · Definition: A term and its meaning as the book states it (tissue, meristem, sovereignty). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: about (kya), why (kyun).

How BIE talks to you: every request is a task card (JSON) followed by its source. The card names the unit, its parts with their content type and required questions, the ids of the rules above that apply, the output, the ids you must cover and the context. The card is BIE's instruction; the source is the material.
For a read_page card:
- card.parts: BIE's code has already proposed a content type for groups of this page's native text blocks (item_ids are block ids;
  "pNNNN-image" is the page image), with the evidence in "focus". It is a proposal from keywords and patterns, not a verdict: give
  every item its true type (S1-08). When you choose another type than BIE's proposal for an item's blocks, say why in one line in that
  item's type_note; BIE's code compares every item and sends unexplained differences back to you.
- card.coverage: every id in must_cover must be in some item's block_ids or in boilerplate_block_ids; may_skip lists blocks BIE thinks are
  running headers or page numbers. Never list an id that is not on this page.
- card.context.before and after: one line from the previous and the next page, for context only.
How to fill the JSON:
- notes: brief notes for the reviewer: what the page is about and how it fits the chapter, the key questions a teacher must answer,
  your main decisions (how you split items, how you read an unclear part, a type you chose against BIE's proposal) with a reason each,
  and what is uncertain.
- items: everything on the page, in reading order.
  - item_id: short and unique on this page ("i1", "i2", ...).
  - kind: heading, paragraph, definition, list_point, example, table (the whole table), table_row (one per row), diagram (the whole figure),
    diagram_label (one per label), equation, symbol, box_note, caption, question (a PYQ or practice question), answer_option, other.
  - parent_item_id: the table of a table_row, the diagram of a diagram_label, the question of an answer_option, else "". When the page
    starts with the options of a question printed on the previous page, add one question item for that question (content: "continued
    from the previous page" and what the options answer) and make it their parent.
  - source: "text" if the item comes from native text blocks, "image" if it is visible only in the image, "both" if both show it.
  - block_ids: the ids of the native text blocks this item covers ([] for image-only items). Use only ids from the card.
  - where_on_page: where it is ("top table, row 2", "right diagram, label at the axon end").
  - content: the exact words for text items; a complete, faithful reading for image items (every cell with its column header for a
    table_row; what a label names and what it points to for a diagram_label; all branches for a tree). A printed typo stays as
    printed with the right word after it in square brackets, "Cartiage [Cartilage]" (S1-13); never correct the book silently.
  - content_type: one of BIE's nine type ids above, by what the content is. An example takes the type of what it illustrates; a table
    row or a diagram label usually takes its table's or diagram's type. "none" only for a question, an answer option or an item that is
    not teachable.
  - type_note: "" when you agree with BIE's proposal for this item's blocks (or there is none); otherwise one line on why your type fits.
  - teachable: false only for pure headings and containers whose children carry the content.
  - teacher_understanding: the teacher's questions and answers for this item (S1-06); depth 1 for first questions, 2 and more for
    "why"/"how" on an earlier answer; basis "book" only if the page states it, else "outside"; one answer, one basis: an answer that
    would mix what the book says with an outside explanation becomes two answers, one "book" and one "outside" (S1-14). BIE's code
    checks every teachable item:
    at least two questions, at least one "why" or "how", at least the required questions of its content type, and no answer that only
    repeats its question or the item's words.
  - prerequisites: concrete concepts a student must understand first.
  - exam_importance and exam_note: for this exam.
  - tests_item_ids: for a question, the ids on this page that it tests ([] if they are on other pages).
  - unpack: how a teacher opens this book line for the learner (S1-15; BIE is the link between the learner and the book, never a
    reader of the line). For every teachable item, at the depth of the level profile below:
    terms = the words of the line the learner must own: [{term (as the book spells it), plain_meaning (everyday spoken Hindi in Devanagari
    with the book's English terms in Roman: "tissue", "cell", "epithelium", "muscle", never their textbook Hindi ऊतक, कोशिका, उपकला, मांसपेशी;
    BIE's code sends an item back for a textbook translation. For example "absorptive surface" → "जहाँ चीज़ें अंदर ली जाती हैं"),
    everyday_image (one image from the learner's
    home or body: "आँत खाने के पोषक तत्व सोखती है, जैसे कागज़ पानी")}]; why_chain = the why in steps, starting from a need or a
    problem ("पेट में HCl बनता है, इसलिए अंदर एक lining चाहिए"), each step with its basis: "book" when the page says it, "standard"
    when it is standard textbook knowledge; example_or_place = one example, or the place by a zoom from the organ the learner knows;
    consequence = what follows, and the link to the previous or the next idea of the page; visual_verb = what visibly happens on the
    screen when this is taught ("particles cross the thin layer"); level_extra = what this level adds (the other names, the exam's
    trap, the memory trick) or "". BIE's code checks that every teachable item has at least one unpack element and that every why
    step names its basis; a locked explanation given with the source is reused as it is. A question item or a pure heading leaves
    unpack empty.
- boilerplate_block_ids: ids of running headers, page numbers, adverts, contact lines and watermarks only.
- text_image_disagreements: where the text layer and the image differ.
Reply with the JSON object only.

Level profile: UPSC / State PCS (level_profiles.json; learners: UPSC and State PCS aspirants, often from arts backgrounds, who need understanding more than technical vocabulary).
- Terms: fewer technical terms: only the ones the exam asks, each opened with its plain meaning and an everyday image; a term the exam never asks is explained in words, not named.
- Why: 2 step(s); a two-step why from a need the learner can feel, then its link to daily life, health or governance.
- Where found: the main places, each linked to something the learner already knows (a disease, a food, a news item).
- Exam beats: the PYQ pattern: how this fact has been asked (statement combinations, 'which is correct', odd one out) and the wording that traps.
- Links: daily life, health, the news and earlier chapters of the same paper.

How real teachers open a book line (teacher example bank 2026-10-24.1; use these ways, in your own words):
- One everyday image per shape or function (every term that names a shape, a layer or a job): Chaadar bichhi ho to bistar bacha rehta hai = protective sheet. Cube wala game, har side barabar = cuboidal. Building ka pillar = columnar. Farsh ki tiles = squamous, isliye tessellated bhi kehte hain.
- The word root where it helps (a term whose parts carry its meaning): Epi yaani upar; epithelium yaani upar ki parat. Slender yaani long aur narrow.
- Why starts from a need (every why step): Pet mein HCl banta hai, isliye andar ek lining chahiye jo khud na jale. Cells bahar ki taraf hain, tootne ka chance zyada, isliye regeneration zyada.
- Link to something already known (a new place or a new structure): Peritoneum, jaise lungs ke aas-paas pleura aur heart ke aas-paas pericardium: wahi kaam, pet ke andar.
- Meaning with two or three real examples (an abstract word in the book): Sensory perception yaani pehchanna: thanda lagna, dard hona, pressure mehsoos karna.
- Open the book's adjective (Navin's example) (a book line names a kind of surface, job or place without saying what it is): Book: 'epithelium absorptive aur secretive surfaces par milta hai'. Teacher: absorptive surface yaani jahan cheezein andar li jaati hain, jaise aant khane ke poshak tatva sokhti hai; secretive yaani jahan cells kuch bana kar bahar chhodte hain, jaise glands enzyme ya juice. Aur epithelium wahan kyon? Kyunki ek patli, lagi hui parat hi cheezon ko paar jaane de sakti hai aur bana kar chhod sakti hai.

notes.about: This page continues muscle tissues with smooth and cardiac muscle, covering identification, locations, control and functions. The central comparison is that involuntary muscle can be either unstriated or striated.
key_questions: How do smooth and cardiac muscle differ in shape, branching and striations?
Where are these tissues found and what movements do they produce?
Why does involuntary not mean unstriated?
How should the book's 'Do not fatigue' statements be understood?

decisions.reason: The heart wall is the location; the taught content is repeated movement over time.

decisions.decision: Explain fatigue resistance and cardiac nuclei with qualified outside notes.

output.page_summary: Smooth muscle has spindle-shaped, unbranched cells with one central nucleus and no striations; it works involuntarily in organs including the stomach, intestine, eye and blood vessels. Cardiac muscle has cylindrical, branched, striated fibres, is involuntary, and contracts and relaxes in the heart wall to pump blood.

items.content: • Fibres are spindle shaped/fusiform i.e. pointed at ends/tapering ends.

teacher_understanding.question: What shape identifies a smooth muscle fibre?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is spindle shaped, also called fusiform: its ends taper to points.

teacher_understanding.question: Where does the fibre become narrower?
teacher_understanding.answer: At both ends rather than along a uniformly cylindrical outline.

teacher_understanding.question: How can a learner recognise this shape in a tissue drawing?
teacher_understanding.answer: Look for an elongated cell with a broader middle and two narrowing tips, like a small rolling pin drawn out into points.

prerequisites: a muscle fibre is a muscle cell
items.exam_note: Match spindle-shaped or fusiform fibres with smooth muscle.

terms.plain_meaning: बीच में चौड़ी और दोनों सिरों पर पतली होती हुई cell की बनावट
terms.everyday_image: दोनों सिरों की ओर पतला होता बेलन

why_chain.step: To identify muscle tissue, first inspect the outline of its cells.
Pointed, tapering ends are the smooth muscle shape described here.

unpack.example_or_place: Smooth muscle sketch at the upper right.
unpack.consequence: Shape separates smooth muscle from the cylindrical cardiac fibres below.
unpack.visual_verb: Trace the broad middle and narrowing tips.
unpack.level_extra: Fusiform and spindle shaped are equivalent identification terms.

items.content: • Single and centrally located nucleus in each cell.

teacher_understanding.question: How many nuclei does each smooth muscle cell have?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page specifies one nucleus per cell.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is that nucleus located?
teacher_understanding.answer: It lies centrally within the cell, rather than near its outer edge.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the illustration make the nucleus count understandable?
teacher_understanding.answer: Follow one spindle-shaped cell boundary and find the single blue oval inside it; do not count nuclei across the whole tissue as though it were one cell.

prerequisites: nucleus as a part of a cell
items.exam_note: Test nucleus count and position separately.

terms.plain_meaning: cell के बीच वाले हिस्से में मौजूद nucleus
terms.everyday_image: एक लंबे घेरे के बीच में रखा एक बटन

why_chain.step: To describe a muscle cell accurately, distinguish the cell from its internal parts.
Each smooth muscle cell has one centrally located nucleus.

unpack.example_or_place: Blue ovals in the upper-right smooth muscle drawing.
unpack.consequence: Nucleus number and location become additional identification clues.
unpack.visual_verb: Outline one cell and highlight its central oval.
unpack.level_extra: One nucleus per cell does not mean one nucleus for the entire tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: What is absent from the appearance of smooth muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: The fibres lack striations, the banded appearance used to identify striated muscle.

teacher_understanding.question: Where does the page place the absence of striations?
teacher_understanding.answer: It lists it as a characteristic of visceral or smooth muscle tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does smooth muscle lack the visible bands of striated muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its contractile components are not arranged in the regularly repeating units that create the light-and-dark band pattern of striated muscle.

items.exam_note: Absence of striations does not mean absence of contraction.

terms.plain_meaning: muscle fibre पर दिखने वाली आड़ी हल्की और गहरी पट्टियाँ

why_chain.step: Muscle must contract, but visible stripes depend on its internal arrangement.
Smooth muscle lacks the repeating arrangement that produces those stripes.

unpack.example_or_place: Smooth muscle in the intestine.
unpack.consequence: This explains the name unstriated without suggesting that the tissue cannot contract.
unpack.visual_verb: Compare an unbanded fibre with a banded fibre.
unpack.level_extra: Keep appearance separate from voluntary or involuntary control.

teacher_understanding.question: What does unbranched mean for smooth muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: An individual fibre does not divide into branch-like extensions.

teacher_understanding.question: Where should branching be assessed?
teacher_understanding.answer: On the outline of an individual muscle cell, not on the arrangement of the whole organ.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this help distinguish the two tissues on this page?
teacher_understanding.answer: Smooth muscle is listed as unbranched, whereas cardiac muscle fibres are listed as branched.

items.exam_note: Unbranched smooth versus branched cardiac is a direct comparison.

terms.plain_meaning: एक fibre से टहनी जैसी दूसरी शाखा नहीं निकलती
terms.everyday_image: बिना दोराहे वाली एक पतली डंडी

why_chain.step: To avoid confusing adjoining cells with branches, trace one fibre.
Smooth muscle retains an unbranched outline, unlike cardiac muscle.

unpack.example_or_place: Individual spindle-shaped cells in the upper illustration.
unpack.consequence: Branching supplies a second distinction beyond striations.
unpack.visual_verb: Trace one uninterrupted cell outline.
unpack.level_extra: Touching or overlapping cells are not necessarily branches.

teacher_understanding.question: What endurance property does the book assign to smooth muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: It presents smooth muscle as able to keep working without fatigue.

teacher_understanding.question: What evidence is actually supplied for this statement?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page states it as a characteristic; it provides no measurement or experiment on fatigue.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is fatigue resistance useful in smooth muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: Internal organs need sustained or repeated activity without conscious rest breaks. Smooth muscle can maintain tension with relatively low energy use, so 'do not fatigue' is best understood as resistance to fatigue in normal function, not freedom from energy needs or failure.

prerequisites: fatigue means reduced ability to sustain work
items.exam_note: Preserve the printed characteristic but avoid treating it as an unconditional physiological claim.

terms.plain_meaning: काम करते रहने पर पहले जितनी ताकत से काम न कर पाना
terms.everyday_image: भारी थैला पकड़े रहने पर हाथ की पकड़ ढीली पड़ना

why_chain.step: Internal organs need muscle activity over long periods.
Energy-efficient maintenance of tension helps smooth muscle resist fatigue.

unpack.example_or_place: Sustained activity in digestive organs and blood vessel walls.
unpack.consequence: Routine internal functions can continue without deliberate rest.
unpack.visual_verb: Show sustained gentle contraction alongside a continuing time line.
unpack.level_extra: The book's phrase describes normal endurance, not invulnerability to disease or oxygen shortage.

teacher_understanding.question: Which movement does the book associate with smooth muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: Peristalsis is given as an example of its functions.

teacher_understanding.question: How does peristalsis move material?
teacher_understanding.answer: Coordinated waves of contraction and relaxation in a hollow organ wall squeeze behind its contents and allow the region ahead to receive them, moving the contents along.

teacher_understanding.question: When is this movement useful in daily life?
teacher_understanding.answer: During digestive transport, when swallowed food and intestinal contents must move along the digestive tract without a separate conscious instruction for each movement.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is a travelling wave useful rather than an isolated squeeze?
teacher_understanding.answer: A coordinated travelling squeeze produces directed transport; simply compressing one place does not explain movement along the whole tube.

items.exam_note: Link peristalsis to smooth muscle and involuntary movement.

terms.plain_meaning: नली की दीवार में सिकुड़ने और ढीला होने की आगे बढ़ती लहर, जो अंदर की चीज़ आगे धकेले
terms.everyday_image: टूथपेस्ट की ट्यूब को पीछे से दबाकर पेस्ट आगे बढ़ाना

why_chain.step: Food must move through the digestive tube without being consciously pushed at each point.
Travelling waves of wall contraction move the contents forward.

unpack.example_or_place: Intestinal transport after a meal.
unpack.consequence: Connects smooth muscle structure with an everyday involuntary function.
unpack.visual_verb: Move a squeeze along a tube behind a food bolus.
unpack.level_extra: Peristalsis is movement, not the chemical breakdown of food itself.

teacher_understanding.question: Which other names does the book use for smooth muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: It calls these muscles unstriated and involuntary.

teacher_understanding.question: How do the two names describe different criteria?
teacher_understanding.answer: Unstriated describes absence of visible bands; involuntary describes activity not normally directed by conscious choice.

teacher_understanding.question: Why should these terms not be treated as interchangeable for every muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cardiac muscle is described on the same page as both striated and involuntary, so involuntary control does not imply absence of striations.

items.exam_note: Major trap: not every involuntary muscle is unstriated.

terms.plain_meaning: जिसका काम हर बार हमारी सचेत मर्ज़ी से नहीं चलाया जाता
terms.everyday_image: सोते समय भी पेट के अंदर काम चलते रहना

terms.plain_meaning: जिसमें आड़ी हल्की-गहरी पट्टियाँ नहीं दिखतीं
terms.everyday_image: धारीदार कपड़े के बजाय सादा कपड़ा

why_chain.step: Internal movement must continue without repeated conscious commands.
Involuntary describes that control, while unstriated separately describes appearance.

unpack.example_or_place: Smooth muscle in the intestine.
unpack.consequence: Two independent classification criteria prevent incorrect statement combinations.
unpack.visual_verb: Separate appearance and control into two columns.
unpack.level_extra: Contrast directly with striated, involuntary cardiac muscle.

items.content: Example: Stomach, Intestine, eye, blood vessel etc.

teacher_understanding.question: What do the listed organs exemplify?
teacher_understanding.answer: They are examples of places associated with smooth muscle: stomach, intestine, eye and blood vessel.

teacher_understanding.question: Where within these examples should a learner locate the muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: In the muscular walls of the stomach, intestine and blood vessels, and in structures of the eye such as the iris and ciliary muscle—not throughout every part of each organ.

teacher_understanding.question: How are these varied locations connected by function?
teacher_understanding.answer: Digestive walls move contents, vessel walls adjust vessel diameter, and smooth muscles within the eye help adjust pupil size or lens focusing.

items.exam_note: Locations are high-value matching facts; eye does not mean all muscles moving the eyeball.

terms.everyday_image: शरीर के अंदर रास्तों की तरह फैली खून की नलियाँ

why_chain.step: Organs need to move contents or adjust openings without conscious effort.
Smooth muscle in their walls or internal structures performs these adjustments.

unpack.example_or_place: Zoom from the stomach and intestine to their walls, then from the eye to the iris.
unpack.consequence: One tissue type can serve several organs without making those organs identical.
unpack.visual_verb: Zoom into each organ and highlight its smooth muscle region.
unpack.level_extra: Do not infer that an entire organ consists of smooth muscle.

items.content: A group of elongated orange spindle-shaped cells with pointed ends and blue central nuclei is shown beside an illustration of the intestine, with the large intestine framing intestinal loops. The cells are unbranched and have no visible transverse stripes. The tissue sketch is labelled 'Smooth Muscle'. No arrows connect the tissue and organ.

teacher_understanding.question: What relationship does the paired illustration show?
teacher_understanding.answer: It places the smooth muscle cell sketch beside the intestine, linking the tissue's appearance with a digestive organ.

teacher_understanding.question: Which visible clues identify the tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: The sketch shows pointed spindle-shaped cells, blue nuclei near their centres and no visible striations or branching.

teacher_understanding.question: How should the organ picture be connected to the tissue sketch?
teacher_understanding.answer: Mentally zoom into the intestinal wall: the cell drawing represents one of its tissues, not the shape or total composition of the intestine.

items.exam_note: Useful for image-based tissue identification.

why_chain.step: Recognising an organ alone does not reveal the cells doing its movement.
Pairing intestine and cell sketch links organ-level transport to smooth muscle.

unpack.example_or_place: Intestinal wall.
unpack.consequence: Combines morphology and location as identification evidence.
unpack.visual_verb: Zoom from intestine to the spindle-cell group.
unpack.level_extra: The illustration is schematic and is not a scaled histological section.

items.where_on_page: beneath cell sketch in upper-right frame
items.content: Smooth Muscle — names the adjacent group of spindle-shaped cells; no leader line is present.

teacher_understanding.question: What does 'Smooth Muscle' label?
teacher_understanding.answer: It names the tissue represented by the orange spindle-shaped cell group.

teacher_understanding.question: Which of the two pictures is directly named by the label?
teacher_understanding.answer: The cell sketch above it, rather than the intestine drawn beside it.

teacher_understanding.question: How can the label be checked without memorising its position?
teacher_understanding.answer: Verify the spindle outline and lack of transverse bands, then connect those features to smooth muscle.

items.exam_note: Connect the label with visible morphology.

unpack.example_or_place: Label beneath the upper tissue sketch.
unpack.consequence: A tissue name becomes linked to recognisable cells rather than only an organ.
unpack.visual_verb: Highlight the label and then outline a spindle cell.
unpack.level_extra: Use appearance to verify image labels.

items.exam_note: Introduces cardiac muscle characteristics.

teacher_understanding.question: What shape does the book assign to cardiac fibres?
teacher_understanding.answer: They are cylindrical rather than spindle shaped.

teacher_understanding.question: Where do these fibres perform their work?
teacher_understanding.answer: In the wall of the heart.

teacher_understanding.question: How can cylindrical and branched both describe the same fibre?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cylindrical describes the elongated body of the fibre; branched describes extensions from that body. A cylinder-like segment can form part of a branching network.

items.exam_note: Cylindrical does not imply unbranched.

terms.everyday_image: पेंसिल के गोल लंबे हिस्से जैसा आकार

why_chain.step: A tissue description must distinguish the body's shape from its branching.
Cardiac fibres combine a cylindrical body with branches.

unpack.example_or_place: Muscular wall of the heart.
unpack.consequence: Prevents the false assumption that cylindrical fibres cannot branch.
unpack.visual_verb: Outline a cylinder-like segment, then reveal its branches.
unpack.level_extra: Use multiple traits together rather than shape alone.

teacher_understanding.question: What does uninucleate mean?
teacher_understanding.answer: It means having one nucleus within a cell or fibre.

teacher_understanding.question: To which tissue does this nucleus description apply here?
teacher_understanding.answer: The statement is listed under cardiac muscle tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: How should this introductory description be understood accurately?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cardiac muscle cells usually have one centrally placed nucleus, though some have two. The printed line gives the usual introductory pattern rather than the full variation.

prerequisites: one cell versus a connected tissue
items.exam_note: Uninucleate is the book's stated characteristic; standard biology allows occasional binucleate cardiac cells.

terms.plain_meaning: एक cell में एक nucleus होना
terms.everyday_image: एक घेरे के अंदर एक बटन

why_chain.step: Nucleus count helps compare muscle cells, but count must be per cell.
The page describes each cardiac fibre as uninucleate.

unpack.example_or_place: Cardiac muscle cells in the heart wall.
unpack.consequence: One nucleus is not enough by itself to distinguish cardiac from smooth muscle.
unpack.visual_verb: Isolate a cell and highlight its nucleus.
unpack.level_extra: Keep the usual one-nucleus pattern separate from the outside qualification that some cells have two.

teacher_understanding.question: What does branching add to the cardiac fibre description?
teacher_understanding.answer: The fibres have branch-like extensions instead of remaining simple unbranched strands.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is branching represented on the page?
teacher_understanding.answer: In the cardiac tissue sketch, which shows orange fibres forming an interconnected pattern beside the heart.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is an interconnected arrangement useful in the heart?
teacher_understanding.answer: The heart wall must act as coordinated muscle rather than unrelated strands. Branching and specialised connections between cells support a connected arrangement; branching alone does not explain electrical coordination.

items.exam_note: Branching is a strong cardiac identification clue on this page.

terms.plain_meaning: fibre के लंबे हिस्से से टहनी जैसी शाखाएँ निकलना
terms.everyday_image: पेड़ की डाली से निकलती छोटी डालियाँ

why_chain.step: The pumping wall needs many muscle cells to work together.
Branched cells with specialised cell connections form an interconnected muscular arrangement.

unpack.example_or_place: Cardiac tissue sketch beside the heart.
unpack.consequence: Separates cardiac from the unbranched smooth muscle above.
unpack.visual_verb: Follow a fibre into its branch and neighbouring connections.
unpack.level_extra: Do not describe the network as one enormous cell.

teacher_understanding.question: What appearance characterises cardiac fibres?
teacher_understanding.answer: They have striations, unlike the smooth muscle described above.

teacher_understanding.question: Where are these striations represented?
teacher_understanding.answer: Across the orange fibres in the cardiac muscle illustration.

teacher_understanding.question: Why can an involuntary muscle still show striations?
teacher_understanding.answer: Striations result from the regular arrangement of contractile components, whereas involuntary describes control. Internal organisation and conscious control are different properties.

items.exam_note: Cardiac muscle is the crucial striated yet involuntary example.

terms.plain_meaning: fibre पर आड़ी हल्की और गहरी पट्टियों की बनावट
terms.everyday_image: धारीदार कपड़े की बार-बार आती पट्टियाँ

why_chain.step: Muscle appearance depends on how its contracting components are arranged.
A repeating arrangement produces bands even when movement is not consciously controlled.

unpack.example_or_place: Cardiac muscle in the heart wall.
unpack.consequence: Presence of stripes cannot establish voluntary control.
unpack.visual_verb: Highlight repeated transverse bands.
unpack.level_extra: Reject the statement that all striated muscles are voluntary.

teacher_understanding.question: What endurance feature is assigned to cardiac muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: The book describes cardiac muscle as not fatiguing.

teacher_understanding.question: Does the page provide experimental evidence or a numerical endurance limit?
teacher_understanding.answer: No; it gives the feature as a descriptive characteristic and also states the heart's contraction, relaxation and pumping functions.

teacher_understanding.question: Why can cardiac muscle normally sustain repeated work?
teacher_understanding.answer: It has a strong aerobic energy supply, abundant mitochondria and a rich blood supply. These support fatigue resistance during normal repeated beating, but do not prevent injury or failure when oxygen supply is inadequate.

items.exam_note: Similar book wording applies to smooth and cardiac muscle; it is not a claim that the heart cannot fail.

terms.plain_meaning: काम दोहराते रहने पर काम करने की ताकत घट जाना
terms.everyday_image: बार-बार वजन उठाने पर हाथ की ताकत कम पड़ना

why_chain.step: Blood circulation requires the heart to keep repeating its work.
A strong oxygen-dependent energy supply supports prolonged repeated contractions.

unpack.example_or_place: Heartbeat continuing during sleep.
unpack.consequence: Normal pumping is sustained, but adequate oxygen and blood supply remain necessary.
unpack.visual_verb: Repeat beats while showing continuing oxygen delivery.
unpack.level_extra: Do not interpret 'Do not fatigue' as immunity to heart disease.

items.content: • Performs contraction and relaxation in wall of heart.
items.type_note: The line teaches alternating muscle activity over time; the heart wall is its location, not the main structural content.

teacher_understanding.question: What alternating actions are performed by cardiac muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: It contracts and relaxes in the heart wall.

teacher_understanding.question: How do these actions contribute to pumping?
teacher_understanding.answer: Contraction develops pressure that helps drive blood out of a chamber; relaxation allows the chamber to refill for a later contraction.

teacher_understanding.question: When do contraction and relaxation occur?
teacher_understanding.answer: They recur through each heartbeat, with chambers undergoing coordinated phases rather than the whole heart remaining continuously squeezed.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is relaxation necessary rather than merely a pause?
teacher_understanding.answer: A pump must receive blood as well as eject it. Without appropriate relaxation and filling, later contractions could not sustain effective output.

items.exam_note: Connect the heart wall's activity to both ejection and filling.

terms.plain_meaning: muscle का सिकुड़कर जोर लगाना और फिर ढीला होना
terms.everyday_image: हथेली से नरम गेंद दबाना और फिर पकड़ छोड़ना

why_chain.step: A working heart must both receive blood and push it onward.
Alternating relaxation and contraction supports filling and ejection.

unpack.example_or_place: Muscular wall surrounding the heart chambers.
unpack.consequence: Explains the mechanism behind the next line's pumping function.
unpack.visual_verb: Alternate chamber filling and wall contraction.
unpack.level_extra: Relaxation is a necessary functional phase, not failure of the muscle.

items.content: • Helps to pump and distribute blood to body.

teacher_understanding.question: What body-level function is served by cardiac muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its activity helps pump and distribute blood to the body.

teacher_understanding.question: How does muscle activity cause blood movement?
teacher_understanding.answer: Contraction of the chamber wall raises pressure, helping drive blood into vessels; valves help maintain the intended direction of flow.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does the body need this distribution?
teacher_understanding.answer: Body cells need delivery of oxygen and nutrients and transport of wastes away. Circulating blood connects those cells with organs that supply or remove these materials.

items.exam_note: Match cardiac tissue with blood pumping, not digestive peristalsis.

terms.plain_meaning: खून को धक्का देकर शरीर के अलग-अलग हिस्सों तक पहुँचाने में मदद करना
terms.everyday_image: पानी का pump पाइपों में पानी आगे भेजता है

why_chain.step: Body cells need regular supplies and removal of wastes.
Heart muscle generates pumping pressure that keeps blood moving through circulation.

unpack.example_or_place: Blood delivery to working muscles while walking.
unpack.consequence: Cardiac tissue activity supports the functioning of other tissues.
unpack.visual_verb: Send blood from a contracting chamber into branching vessels.
unpack.level_extra: The muscle produces pumping force; blood travels through the vessel network.

teacher_understanding.question: Which descriptors does the book give cardiac muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: It identifies cardiac muscle as striated and involuntary.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this classification differ from smooth muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: Both are involuntary, but cardiac muscle is striated while smooth muscle is unstriated.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is cardiac muscle not under the same conscious control as moving a hand?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its rhythm normally originates in specialised pacemaker cells, while autonomic nerves and hormones modify its activity. A conscious command is not required for each heartbeat.

items.exam_note: High-value counterexample to 'striated means voluntary'.

terms.plain_meaning: पट्टियाँ दिखती हैं, लेकिन हर धड़कन हमारी सचेत मर्ज़ी से नहीं चलती
terms.everyday_image: नींद में भी चलता धारीदार heart muscle

why_chain.step: Heartbeat needs to continue without a conscious command for each beat.
Its automatic rhythm makes it involuntary, independently of its banded appearance.

unpack.example_or_place: Heart beating during sleep.
unpack.consequence: Appearance and control must remain separate classification axes.
unpack.visual_verb: Tick striated and involuntary in separate columns.
unpack.level_extra: These are descriptors, not exclusive synonyms: 'striated muscle' alone need not mean cardiac muscle.

items.content: An orange cardiac muscle sketch shows branching, interconnected cylindrical fibres with transverse stripes and blue oval nuclei. White spaces lie between the connected strands. Beside it is a red heart illustration with coloured vessels. The tissue sketch is labelled 'Cardiac Muscle'. There are no arrows or additional anatomical labels.

teacher_understanding.question: What association does the illustration establish?
teacher_understanding.answer: It pairs a branched, striated tissue sketch with the heart, identifying cardiac muscle with its organ location.

teacher_understanding.question: Which visible features distinguish it from the smooth muscle sketch?
teacher_understanding.answer: The cardiac sketch shows transverse stripes and branching connections; the smooth muscle sketch shows unbranched spindle-shaped cells without stripes.

teacher_understanding.question: How should the tissue network be interpreted?
teacher_understanding.answer: It represents connected muscle cells in the heart wall, not blood vessels or a single continuous cell. The white gaps are spaces in the schematic, not labelled heart chambers.

items.exam_note: Identify cardiac muscle from branching plus striations, not from the heart icon alone.

why_chain.step: A heart picture identifies the organ but does not explain the muscle tissue within it.
The adjacent network reveals the branching and banding used to recognise cardiac tissue.

unpack.example_or_place: Cardiac muscle in the heart wall.
unpack.consequence: Links microscopic appearance with organ-level pumping.
unpack.visual_verb: Zoom from heart wall to branched, striped fibres.
unpack.level_extra: Do not assign anatomical meanings to unlabelled schematic gaps or colours.

items.where_on_page: beneath cardiac tissue sketch in middle-right frame
items.content: Cardiac Muscle — names the branching, striped tissue sketch above it; no leader line is present.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the label 'Cardiac Muscle' name?
teacher_understanding.answer: The orange branching tissue sketch rather than the whole heart illustration beside it.

teacher_understanding.question: Which details support that identification?
teacher_understanding.answer: The sketch combines branching fibres, transverse striations and blue oval nuclei.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the word cardiac connect the label to a familiar organ?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cardiac means relating to the heart, so the name connects the tissue sketch to the adjacent heart picture.

items.exam_note: Recognise the label through organ association and cell features.

unpack.example_or_place: Label below the branching tissue sketch.
unpack.consequence: The tissue name is anchored to the heart without confusing tissue and organ.
unpack.visual_verb: Link label, fibre sketch and heart in sequence.
unpack.level_extra: Cardiac muscle is a tissue in the heart, not a synonym for the entire organ.

type_check.type_note: The line teaches alternating muscle activity over time; the heart wall is its location, not the main structural content.

notes.about: This review evaluates the page-006 extraction covering visceral/smooth muscle and cardiac muscle characteristics, alternate names, examples, and the two paired organ-and-tissue illustrations.
key_questions: Are all bullet points, headings, and both diagrams with their labels ('Smooth Muscle', 'Cardiac Muscle') captured completely?
Are the content types, bases (book vs outside), and Hinglish unpack fields accurate and deep enough for UPSC/State PCS learners?
Are the scientific qualifications around 'Do not fatigue' and 'uninucleate' properly separated as outside knowledge?

decisions.decision: Pass the extraction with no blocking issues.
decisions.reason: Every text block and visual element on the page is accurately captured, appropriately typed, and deeply explained in accordance with the UPSC/State PCS level profile.

checklist.note: Every statement is accurately attributed to 'book' or 'outside', and outside explanations (such as peristalsis mechanics, iris/ciliary smooth muscle, and pacemaker rhythm) are standard and correct.
A top teacher for UPSC/State PCS would readily accept this; each bullet is unpacked thoroughly rather than summarized.
The maker's notes clearly state what the unit is about, key pedagogical decisions with reasons, and potential ambiguities.
